claim: Most of our knowledge on human CNS circuitry and related disorders originates from model organisms.
source: Most of our knowledge on human CNS circuitry and related disorders originates from model organisms.

claim: Human brain slice cultures derived from neurosurgical resections may offer novel avenues to approach the translational gap between model organisms and humans.
source: Human brain slice cultures derived from neurosurgical resections may offer novel avenues to approach this translational gap.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential application of the model system.

claim: The study demonstrates robust preservation of complex neuronal cytoarchitecture in long-term brain slice cultures.
source: We now demonstrate robust preservation of the complex neuronal cytoarchitecture and electrophysiological properties of human pyramidal neurons in long-term brain slice cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including morphological reconstructions and measurements.

claim: The study demonstrates robust preservation of electrophysiological properties of human pyramidal neurons in long-term brain slice cultures.
source: We now demonstrate robust preservation of the complex neuronal cytoarchitecture and electrophysiological properties of human pyramidal neurons in long-term brain slice cultures.

claim: The study delineates optimal conditions for efficient viral transduction of human brain slice cultures.
source: Further experiments delineate the optimal conditions for efficient viral transduction of cultures
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing successful AAV transduction as shown in Figure 2 and related experiments.

claim: Viral transduction enables 'high throughput' fluorescence-mediated 3D reconstruction of genetically targeted neurons at comparable quality to state-of-the-art biocytin fillings.
source: enabling 'high throughput' fluorescence-mediated 3D reconstruction of genetically targeted neurons at comparable quality to state-of-the-art biocytin fillings
evidence: This is supported by comparative data between GFP-labeled and biocytin-filled neurons shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The study demonstrates feasibility of long term live cell imaging of human cells in vitro.
source: and demonstrate feasibility of long term live cell imaging of human cells in vitro.

claim: The human brain is composed of an intricate network of diverse cell types with complex interactions and connections.
source: The human brain is composed of an intricate network of diverse cell types with complex interactions and connections (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Somogyi et al., 1998).

claim: The microstructure within the brain was appreciated in early pioneering work by Santiago Ramón y Cajal.
source: The microstructure within the brain was already appreciated in the early pioneering work by Santiago Ramón y Cajal
evidence: This is a historical reference to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Brain microstructure has been investigated in post mortem human brain samples.
source: and has been further investigated in the last decades in post mortem human brain samples (Elston and DeFelipe, 2002; Elston et al., 2001)

claim: Brain microstructure has been investigated in numerous animal models.
source: and in numerous animal models (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Somogyi et al., 1998).

claim: Neurons function as a core component of the microstructure of CNS circuits.
source: Neurons function as a core component of the microstructure of CNS circuits.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons (pyramidal neurons) constitute 80% of the human neocortex.

claim: GABAergic interneurons constitute 20% of the human neocortex.

claim: Cortical pyramidal neurons can be categorized into four classes according to their output connectivity.
source: Cortical pyramidal neurons can be further categorized into four classes according to their output connectivity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge, with further details provided in the text.

claim: Intratelencephalic pyramidal neurons are distributed throughout cortical layers 2–6.
source: Intratelencephalic pyramidal neurons are distributed throughout cortical layers 2–6 and build associative connections with other cortical areas (within one hemisphere or across the corpus callosum) or with the striatum.

claim: Intratelencephalic pyramidal neurons build associative connections with other cortical areas or with the striatum.
source: Intratelencephalic pyramidal neurons are distributed throughout cortical layers 2–6 and build associative connections with other cortical areas (within one hemisphere or across the corpus callosum) or with the striatum.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Pyramidal tract neurons reside in layer five.
source: Pyramidal tract neurons reside in layer five and project their axons to the brain stem and spinal cord.

claim: Pyramidal tract neurons project their axons to the brain stem and spinal cord.
source: Pyramidal tract neurons reside in layer five and project their axons to the brain stem and spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Corticothalamic neurons establish axonal output connectivity from layer six to area related thalamic nuclei.
source: Corticothalamic neurons establish axonal output connectivity from layer six to area related thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Layer four short-axon intratelencephalic neurons locally relay thalamic input.
source: The fourth category comprises layer four short-axon intratelencephalic neurons, which locally relay thalamic input (Shepherd and Rowe, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: With the exception of layer four intratelencephalic neurons in sensory areas (spiny stellate cells), pyramidal neurons typically show a long apical dendrite.
source: With the exception of layer four intratelencephalic neurons in sensory areas (spiny stellate cells) pyramidal neurons typically show a long apical dendrite.

source: Overall morphology and complexity of apical and basal dendrites can substantially differ between pyramidal neurons and throughout layers.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: There exist marked species-specific differences of structural features and functional properties of pyramidal neurons.
source: Furthermore, work by colleagues in the field provides direct evidence that there also exist marked species-specific differences of structural features and functional properties of pyramidal neurons (Mohan et al., 2015)

claim: There are species-specific differences regarding basic cortical properties.
source: as well as regarding basic cortical properties (Eyal et al., 2016)

claim: There are species-specific differences in cell types.
source: cell types (Boldog et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015)

source: functional divergence (Napoli and Obeid, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There are species-specific differences in plasticity mechanisms.
source: and plasticity mechanisms (Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Species-specific differences underscore the challenges of modeling human disease by cellular and animal models.
source: Such differences underscore the challenges of modeling human disease by cellular and animal models and call for the development of new translational approaches based on human nervous tissue.

claim: Spare human CNS tissue obtained from neurosurgical procedures has proven valuable for electrophysiological studies in acute slice preparations.
source: Spare human CNS tissue obtained from neurosurgical procedures has proven valuable throughout the years, for example for electrophysiological studies in acute slice preparations (Bernard et al., 2004; Kalmbach et al., 2018; Kerkhofs et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Past attempts to establish organotypic slice cultures of human CNS tissue had repeatedly faced pronounced limitations regarding viability and integrity.
source: Unlike with rodent CNS tissue, past attempts by different groups to establish organotypic slice cultures of human CNS tissue had yet repeatedly faced pronounced limitations regarding viability and integrity (O'Connor et al., 1997; Verwer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent efforts provided proof-of-concept data on electrophysiological function in human brain slice cultures.
source: However, recent efforts challenged these limitations and provided promising proof-of-concept data on electrophysiological function (Eugène et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Recent efforts provided proof-of-concept data on optogenetic targeting in human brain slice cultures.
source: and optogenetic targeting (Andersson et al., 2016) in human brain slice cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Subsequent studies established successful neuronal labeling, optical manipulation and calcium imaging by virus-driven rapid expression in short term cultures of several days.
source: Subsequent studies established successful neuronal labeling, optical manipulation and calcium imaging by virus-driven rapid expression of respective probes in short term cultures of several days (Ting et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous work by the authors demonstrated that neuronal viability and network activity of human brain slice cultures can be significantly extended to up to three weeks under specified conditions.
source: Recent parallel work by us in contrast focused on optimization of culture conditions and demonstrated that neuronal viability and network activity of human brain slice cultures can be significantly extended to up to three weeks under specified conditions (Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Proper function of complex CNS networks critically depends on morphological and functional integrity of neurons.
source: Proper function of complex CNS networks, however, critically depends on morphological and functional integrity of neurons structurally underlying circuitry.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Neurons need to extend their dendritic processes to correct locations to receive appropriate synaptic inputs and relay them to adequate target structures.
source: Neurons need to extend their dendritic processes to correct locations in order to receive appropriate synaptic inputs and relay them to adequate target structures.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Specific functional properties are required for neurons to compute and integrate information in a meaningful way.
source: Specific functional properties are required to compute and integrate information in a meaningful way.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: It is not known whether morphological complexity and electrophysiological characteristics are maintained in human brain slice cultures over two to three weeks.
source: Whether this level of morphological complexity along with inherent electrophysiological characteristics is maintained in human brain slice cultures over a period of two to three weeks or whether dendritic arbors rarefy and functional features dissipate is not known and will be investigated in this work.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The Cre-lox system has enabled better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
source: In the last decades, important molecular genetic achievements and subsequent combined application of tools such as the Cre-lox system (Song and Palmiter, 2018), optogenetics (Kim et al., 2017; Madisen et al., 2012) and virus-mediated gene targeting/knockout/delivery (Hendrie and Russell, 2005; Howard et al., 2008; Rao and Craig, 1997) enabled an increasingly better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Optogenetics has enabled better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
source: In the last decades, important molecular genetic achievements and subsequent combined application of tools such as the Cre-lox system (Song and Palmiter, 2018), optogenetics (Kim et al., 2017; Madisen et al., 2012) and virus-mediated gene targeting/knockout/delivery (Hendrie and Russell, 2005; Howard et al., 2008; Rao and Craig, 1997) enabled an increasingly better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Virus-mediated gene targeting/knockout/delivery has enabled better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
source: In the last decades, important molecular genetic achievements and subsequent combined application of tools such as the Cre-lox system (Song and Palmiter, 2018), optogenetics (Kim et al., 2017; Madisen et al., 2012) and virus-mediated gene targeting/knockout/delivery (Hendrie and Russell, 2005; Howard et al., 2008; Rao and Craig, 1997) enabled an increasingly better understanding of how distinct cell types assemble and form functional circuitry in the rodent brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adapting genetic strategies to human brain slice cultures will open new roads toward dissection of human CNS circuitry.
source: Adapting such strategies to human brain slice cultures reflecting an environment as close as possible to the actual human brain will open new roads toward dissection of human CNS circuitry and could potentially provide an increasingly more accurate understanding of how human CNS disease develops.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of the model system.

claim: The study performed detailed cellular analyses of the somatodendritic and synaptic spine compartments of single neurons throughout the course of culturing.
source: Toward these aims, we now performed detailed cellular analyses of the somatodendritic and synaptic spine compartments and of characteristic electrophysiological properties of single neurons throughout the course of culturing.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The study performed detailed analyses of characteristic electrophysiological properties of single neurons throughout the course of culturing.
source: Toward these aims, we now performed detailed cellular analyses of the somatodendritic and synaptic spine compartments and of characteristic electrophysiological properties of single neurons throughout the course of culturing.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The study established conditions for efficient viral transduction with a focus on glutamatergic pyramidal neurons within human brain slice cultures.
source: Further experiments established the conditions for efficient viral transduction with a focus on glutamatergic pyramidal neurons within human brain slice cultures.
evidence: This describes experimental work performed in the study.

claim: The study finds robust structural and electrophysiological stability of human pyramidal neurons.
source: We find robust structural and electrophysiological stability of human pyramidal neurons and amenability of human brain slice cultures to efficient genetic manipulation
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human brain slice cultures are amenable to efficient genetic manipulation as revealed by successful transduction by GFP-encoding AAV-vectors.
source: We find robust structural and electrophysiological stability of human pyramidal neurons and amenability of human brain slice cultures to efficient genetic manipulation, as revealed by successful transduction by GFP-encoding adeno-associated viral vectors (AAV-vectors).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings supported by data in Figure 2 and related experiments.

claim: GFP fluorescence levels were sufficient for post-hoc confocal microscopy-based assessment of neuronal morphology including spines.
source: GFP fluorescence levels were sufficient for both post-hoc confocal microscopy- and two-photon live cell imaging-based assessment of neuronal morphology including spines emanating from the dendritic arbors.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 2, 4, 7, and 9.

claim: GFP fluorescence levels were sufficient for two-photon live cell imaging-based assessment of neuronal morphology including spines.
source: GFP fluorescence levels were sufficient for both post-hoc confocal microscopy- and two-photon live cell imaging-based assessment of neuronal morphology including spines emanating from the dendritic arbors.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The study demonstrates GFP-based cellular 3D morphological analysis with increased efficiency and compatible quality compared to classic intracellular biocytin fillings.
source: We demonstrate GFP-based cellular 3D morphological analysis with increased efficiency and compatible quality in comparison to classic intracellular biocytin fillings.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data between GFP and biocytin reconstructions shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Whole cell patch clamp recordings were performed from 45 pyramidal neurons in acute or cultured slices.
source: Besides morphological and structural features intact physiology of neurons constitutes one of the hallmarks of healthy neural tissue. In a first set of experiments we determined the stability of the electrophysiological properties of pyramidal neurons performing whole cell patch clamp recordings (n = 45) from cells in acute (n = 17) or cultured (n = 28) slices (2–14 DIV).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected.

claim: Recordings of pyramidal neurons showed a typical regular spiking pattern in acute and cultured slices.
source: Recordings of pyramidal neurons showed a typical regular spiking pattern in acute and cultured slices (Figure 1B,C), as described in previous studies investigating human pyramidal neurons in acute slices (Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1B,C and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The firing frequency in response to current injections was not significantly different between cells recorded in acute slices and cells in cultures between 2-3 DIV and 7-14 DIV.
source: The firing frequency in response to current injections was not significantly different between the cells recorded on the day of the surgery (acute slices = 0 DIV, with a peak firing rate of 50.84 ± 9.90 Hz in response to a current injection of 200 pA) and the cells in cultures between 2 and 3 DIV (peak firing rate: 59.4 ± 12.46) and 7–14 DIV (peak firing rate of 55.79 ± 9.34 Hz), (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.74, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mean values of AP half width did not differ between cells at 0 DIV, 2-3 DIV and 7-14 DIV.
source: Similarly, mean values of AP half width, sag potential amplitude and input resistance did not differ between the tested groups (0 DIV, 2–3 DIV and 7–14 DIV, Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.05, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mean values of sag potential amplitude did not differ between cells at 0 DIV, 2-3 DIV and 7-14 DIV.
source: Similarly, mean values of AP half width, sag potential amplitude and input resistance did not differ between the tested groups (0 DIV, 2–3 DIV and 7–14 DIV, Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.05, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mean values of input resistance did not differ between cells at 0 DIV, 2-3 DIV and 7-14 DIV.
source: Similarly, mean values of AP half width, sag potential amplitude and input resistance did not differ between the tested groups (0 DIV, 2–3 DIV and 7–14 DIV, Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.05, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no significant linear regression correlation of AP half width, sag potential amplitude and input resistance versus DIV.
source: This was also reflected by no significant linear regression correlation of these parameters versus the DIV (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mean resting membrane potential showed a small significant difference between acutely measured cells and early cultured cells.
source: For mean values of resting membrane potential we found a small significant difference (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05) for the acutely measured cells (0 DIV, −77.94 ± 1.5 mV) in comparison to early cultured (2–3 DIV, −72.38 ± 0.96 mV, Dunn's multiple comparisons test, *p=0.02)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Mean resting membrane potential showed a small significant difference between acutely measured cells and late in culture cells.
source: and late in culture cells (7-14 DIV, 71.95 ± 1.43, Dunn's multiple comparisons test, *p=0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: There was no significant difference in resting membrane potential between early (2-3 DIV) and late in culture (7-14 DIV) measured cells.
source: However, there was no significant difference between early (2–3 DIV) and late in culture (7–14 DIV) measured cells (Dunn's multiple comparisons test, p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: There was no significant linear regression correlation of resting potential versus DIV for cells of all three groups.
source: This was also reflected by no significant linear regression correlation of the resting potential versus the DIV for cells of all three groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increasing time in culture does not impact the majority of analyzed intrinsic electrophysiological characteristics of pyramidal neurons, except for membrane resting potential.
source: In summary, increasing time in culture does not impact the majority of analyzed intrinsic electrophysiological characteristics of pyramidal neurons, except for the membrane resting potential which slightly changed to more depolarized values within the first 2–3 days in culture and then stayed stable over the remaining time.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the electrophysiological data presented.

claim: Membrane resting potential slightly changed to more depolarized values within the first 2-3 days in culture and then stayed stable.
source: In summary, increasing time in culture does not impact the majority of analyzed intrinsic electrophysiological characteristics of pyramidal neurons, except for the membrane resting potential which slightly changed to more depolarized values within the first 2–3 days in culture and then stayed stable over the remaining time.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the electrophysiological data presented.

claim: Satb2 is a transcription factor that is expressed exclusively in excitatory neurons in adult mouse and human cortex.
source: Satb2 is a transcription factor that is expressed exclusively in excitatory neurons in adult mouse and human cortex (Britanova et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2013; Hodge et al., 2019; http://celltypes.brain-map.org/rnaseq).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and a database reference.

claim: No significant changes in absolute numbers of Map2/Satb2 double-positive neurons were found in slice cultures between 0 DIV, 9 DIV and 14 DIV.
source: Taking advantage of Map2, a neuron-specific cytoskeletal protein, in combination with Satb2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) we found no significant changes of the absolute numbers of double-positive neurons in slice cultures between 0 DIV (3 slices), 9 DIV (3 slices) and 14 DIV (2 slices) (Dunn's multiple comparisons test, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absolute number of Map2 and Satb2 double positive neurons per 10000 µm2 was on average 8.57 ± 0.60 in acute slices.
source: the absolute number of Map2 and Satb2 double positive neurons per 100 µm × 100 µm (10000 µm2) was on average 8.57 ± 0.60 in acute slices (18 analyzed areas)
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The absolute number of Map2 and Satb2 double positive neurons per 10000 µm2 was on average 10.14 ± 3.52 in slices analyzed at 9 DIV.
source: 10.14 ± 3.52 (16 analyzed areas) in slices analyzed at 9 DIV
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The absolute number of Map2 and Satb2 double positive neurons per 10000 µm2 was on average 9.49 ± 1.77 in slices obtained at 14 DIV.
source: and 9.49 ± 1.77 (9 analyzed areas) in slices obtained at 14 DIV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The ratio of Satb2 and Map2 double-positive neurons to all Map2 positive neurons was 0.72 ± 0.02 in acute slices.
source: Ratios were 0.72 ± 0.02 in acute slices
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The ratio of Satb2 and Map2 double-positive neurons to all Map2 positive neurons was 0.59 ± 0.09 at 9 DIV.
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The ratio of Satb2 and Map2 double-positive neurons to all Map2 positive neurons was 0.65 ± 0.11 at 14 DIV.
source: and 0.65 ± 0.11 at 14 DIV
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: The ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurons at 9 DIV was discretely lower but statistically significant compared to 0 DIV.
source: and revealed a discretely lower, albeit statistically significant, ratio at 9 DIV compared to 0 DIV, but no difference between 0 DIV and 14 DIV or 9 DIV compared to 14 DIV (Dunn's multiple comparisons test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of immunocytochemistry data.

claim: There was no difference in the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurons between 0 DIV and 14 DIV.
source: but no difference between 0 DIV and 14 DIV or 9 DIV compared to 14 DIV (Dunn's multiple comparisons test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of immunocytochemistry data.

claim: There was no difference in the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurons between 9 DIV and 14 DIV.
source: but no difference between 0 DIV and 14 DIV or 9 DIV compared to 14 DIV (Dunn's multiple comparisons test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of immunocytochemistry data.

claim: The data indicate robust survival of excitatory and inhibitory neurons with a sustained ratio throughout the culturing time.
source: These data indicate robust survival of excitatory and inhibitory neurons with a sustained ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurons throughout the culturing time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunocytochemistry data presented.

claim: Retrograde AAV encoding GFP under the human synapsin promoter was used to specifically transduce neurons.
source: To investigate whether neurons in human brain slice cultures can be genetically targeted with viral vectors and whether such strategies could render morphological analysis of human neurons more efficient than approaches solely relying on classic biocytin fillings, we used retrograde adeno-associated virus (AAVrg) encoding GFP under the human synapsin promoter to specifically transduce neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: Slices were injected with virus at 3-5 DIV and cells were recorded and imaged at 8-16 DIV.
source: The slices were injected with the virus at 3–5 DIV using a picospritzer, cells were then recorded and imaged at 8–16 DIV (n = 20 slices).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: Robust virus transduction was found in all injected slices with variable expression in distinct types of neurons throughout all cortical layers.
source: We found robust virus transduction in all injected slices with variable expression in distinct types of neurons throughout all cortical layers (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: GFP expression was clearly present in somata, dendrites including spines and axons of transduced neurons.
source: The GFP expression was clearly present in somata, dendrites including spines and axons of transduced neurons (Figure 2A1 and A2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A1 and A2.

claim: GFP expression levels were found to be very robust, enabling quantification of whole cell morphology, spine density, spine head diameter and spine length.
source: GFP expression levels were found to be very robust, suggesting that several types of analyses including quantification of whole cell morphology, spine density, spine head diameter and spine length (see below) could be achieved based on GFP fluorescence.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent morphological analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: 24 biocytin fillings were deemed to be of sufficient quality to enable high-resolution morphological analysis.
source: Pyramidal neurons were filled with biocytin during electrophysiological recordings and 24 fillings were deemed to be of sufficient quality (clear presence of both apical and basal dendritic compartments, Figure 1A, while incompletely filled neurons were excluded from the analysis) to enable high-resolution morphological analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the data set used for morphological analysis.

claim: Reconstructed neurons were classified by the distance of their soma to the pia as layers 2/3 (distance to pia: 300-1200 µm, n=16), layer 4 (distance to pia: 1200-1500 µm, n=3) or layers 5/6 (distance to pia: 1500-2900 µm, n=5) pyramidal neurons.
source: Reconstructed neurons were classified by the distance of their soma to the pia as layers 2/3 (distance to pia: 300–1200 µm, n = 16), layer 4 (distance to pia: 1200–1500 µm, n = 3) or layers 5/6 (distance to pia: 1500–2900 µm, n = 5) pyramidal neurons (Figure 3) (Mohan et al., 2015; Ting et al., 2018; Goriounova et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the classification system used, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: All reconstructed neurons presented a typical pyramidal neuronal shape with distinct apical dendrites, extensive basal dendritic trees, axons and spines.
source: All neurons presented a typical pyramidal neuronal shape with distinct apical dendrites (Figure 3, red), extensive basal dendritic trees (Figure 3, blue), axons (Figure 3, magenta) and spines present on the apical and basal dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no significant correlation between total basal, apical or combined dendritic length and the number of days in vitro for biocytin filled neurons.
source: There was no significant correlation between the total basal, apical or combined dendritic length and the number of days in vitro for these analyzed biocytin filled neurons (n = 24, linear regression, p=0.07).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of morphological data.

claim: There was no significant correlation of total dendritic length parameters with overall soma distance to the pia for all neurons.
source: While there was also no significant correlation of all three parameters of total dendritic length with overall soma distance to the pia (n = 24)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of morphological data.

claim: Subgroup analysis of layers 2/3 neurons revealed a gradually increasing total length of apical and basal dendrites with increasing depth.
source: additional subgroup analysis of superficially and incrementally deeper situated layers 2/3 neurons in acute and cultured cortical tissue revealed a gradually increasing total length of apical and basal dendrites (Figure 5A; n = 16), as has been described in a previous study by Mohan et al. (2015) in non-cultured CNS tissue.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5A and comparison to prior literature.

claim: 23 GFP positive neurons were picked from four virally transduced slices (8, 9, 10 and 14 DIV) with strong GFP expression in layers 2-6.
source: We picked a total of 23 neurons from four virally transduced slices (8, 9, 10 and 14 DIV) with strong GFP expression in layers 2–6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the data set used for GFP-based morphological analysis.

claim: All 23 GFP positive neurons were classified by the distance of their soma to the pia as layers 2/3 (n=12), layer 4 (n=3) or layers 5/6 (n=8) pyramidal neurons.
source: Similar to biocytin filled neurons all 23 GFP positive neurons were classified by the distance of their soma to the pia as layers 2/3 (distance to pia: 300–1200 µm, n = 12), layer 4 (distance to pia: 1200–1500 µm, n = 3) or layers 5/6 (distance to pia: 1500–2900 µm, n = 8) pyramidal neurons (Figure 4; apical dendrites, red; basal dendrites, blue; axons, magenta).
evidence: This describes the classification of GFP-labeled neurons.

claim: GFP-mediated tracing successfully detected the gradually increasing dendritic length of layers 2/3 neurons depending on their soma position.
source: In comparison to biocytin fillings GFP-mediated tracing equally successfully detected the gradually increasing dendritic length of layers 2/3 neurons depending on their soma position (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between combined dendritic length and DIV for GFP-based tracings.
source: There was no significant correlation between the combined dendritic length and the DIV, neither for GFP-based tracings (data not shown)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of morphological data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between combined dendritic length and DIV after pooling all biocytin and GFP reconstructed neurons.
source: nor for analysis after pooling all biocytin and GFP reconstructed neurons (Figure 5C, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GFP-based reconstructions slightly underestimated combined total dendritic length compared to biocytin fillings (p<0.01).
source: Comparing combined total dendritic length of all biocytin and GFP-labeled neurons independent of the DIV revealed a slight underestimation of values by GFP (Figure 5C, right panel, p<0.01, n = 24 (biocytin), n = 23 (GFP), unpaired Mann Whitney test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The underestimation by GFP is likely because very distal dendritic ramifications are captured less reliably.
source: – likely because very distal dendritic ramifications are being captured somewhat less reliably (due to intermingling GFP positive processes from neighboring neurons and some arising uncertainty when judging whether to assign GFP positive processes in the periphery of the neuron being reconstructed to the filament of this neuron or whether to discard them by deeming them as originating from neighboring neurons)
evidence: This is an interpretation/speculation about the cause of the observed difference.

claim: GFP-based reconstruction successfully captured the major parts of dendritic arbors.
source: – but overall successful reconstruction of the major parts of dendritic arbors (Figure 2 and Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: A total of 47 biocytin and GFP-labeled neurons have been analyzed.
source: In summary a total of 47 biocytin and GFP-labeled neurons have been analyzed (Figures 3–5)
evidence: This is a summary of the morphological analysis data set.

claim: The morphological analysis revealed remarkable structural preservation of pyramidal neurons without clear signs of declining morphological complexity.
source: In summary a total of 47 biocytin and GFP-labeled neurons have been analyzed (Figures 3–5), revealing remarkable structural preservation of pyramidal neurons without clear signs of declining morphological complexity.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the morphological data.

claim: The data indicate absence of widespread progressing neuronal degeneration throughout the time in culture.
source: These data not only indicate absence of widespread progressing neuronal degeneration throughout the time in culture
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological stability data.

claim: The data demonstrate genetic labeling as a valid alternative approach to 3D morphological analysis of adult human neurons with significantly increased efficiency compared to classic single cell biocytin fillings.
source: but also demonstrate genetic labeling as a valid alternative approach to 3D morphological analysis of adult human neurons with significantly increased efficiency in comparison to classic single cell biocytin fillings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative morphological analysis data.

claim: Qualitative assessment of calretinin staining at 0 DIV and 9 DIV demonstrated survival of at least this subset of interneurons.
source: To further investigate beyond our earlier indirect assessment based on the ratio of Map2 and Satb2 double-positive neurons to all Map2 positive neurons, whether also interneurons survive in human brain slice cultures we first performed immunocytochemical stainings for calretinin. Unlike for other interneuron subtype identifiers, we were able to obtain reliable stainings for calretinin in acute and cultured human brain slice tissue. Qualitative assessment at 0 DIV and at 9 DIV demonstrated survival of at least this subset of interneurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Intracellular recordings were performed of 22 neurons that were identified morphologically or electrophysiologically as interneurons.
source: Next, we performed intracellular recordings of 22 neurons that were identified morphologically or electrophysiologically as interneurons (Figure 6A,B,D).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected for interneurons.

claim: For resting membrane potential, input resistance, AP half width and sag potential, no significant differences were found between interneurons measured in acute slices and in cultured slices at 7-14 DIV.
source: For all these parameters we did not find significant differences between neurons measured in acute (n = 7) and in cultured slices at 7–14 DIV (n = 15) (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figures 6D-G.

claim: The firing behavior of recorded interneurons showed distinct properties ranging from fast spiking to non-fast spiking firing patterns.
source: The firing behavior of the recorded interneurons showed distinct properties as described before for rodents and humans and ranged from fast spiking (Figure 6D) to none fast spiking firing patterns (Ascoli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6D and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in acute and cultured slices revealed no significant differences on average regarding spine density.
source: Pyramidal neurons in acute (0 DIV) and cultured slices (2 DIV - 14 DIV) revealed no significant differences on average regarding spine density (acute and filled with biocytin: 0.54 ± 0.04 spines/µm, n = 5; cultured and filled with biocytin: 0.53 ± 0.04 spines/µm, p=0.99, n = 17; cultured and GFP-labeled: 0.44 ± 0.05, p=0.19, n = 11; Kruskis Wallis Test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of spine morphology data.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in acute and cultured slices revealed no significant differences on average regarding spine length.
source: spine length (acute biocytin: 1.46 ± 0.04 µm, n = 5; cultured biocytin: 1.54 ± 0.08 µm, n = 17, p=0.87; cultured GFP-labeled: 1.60 ± 0.05 µm, n = 11, p=0.45; Kruskis Wallis Test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of spine morphology data.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in acute and cultured slices revealed no significant differences on average regarding spine head diameter.
source: or spine head diameter (acute biocytin: 0.47 ± 0.05 µm, n = 5; cultured biocytin: 0.52 ± 0.02 µm, p=052, n = 17; cultured GFP-labeled: 0.58 ± 0.04 µm, p=0.09, n = 11; Kruskis Wallis Test) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A moderate negative correlation was found between spine density and DIV (r2 = -0.21, p<0.01).
source: We found a moderate negative correlation between the spine density and the DIV (Figure 7E, linear regression, r2 = −0.21, p<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A moderate positive correlation was found between spine head diameter and DIV (r2 = 0.15, p<0.05).
source: and a moderate positive correlation between the spine head diameter and the DIV (Figure 7E, linear regression, r2 = 0.15, p<0.05)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Average spine length showed no correlation to DIV.
source: while the average spine length showed no correlation to the DIV (Figure 7E, linear regression, p=0.99).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A strong positive correlation was found between the distance of neuronal somata to the pia and spine length (r2 = 0.46, p<0.001).
source: In addition, we found a strong positive correlation between the distance of neuronal somata to the pia and the spine length (Figure 7F, linear regression, r2 = 0.46, p<0.001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: No correlation was found between distance to pia and spine head diameter.
source: but not to the spine head diameter (Figure 7F, linear regression, p=0.06)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: No correlation was found between distance to pia and spine density.
source: or spine density (Figure 7F, linear regression, p=0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The analyses revealed mild changes at most on spine level without clear indication of prevalent alterations related to the culturing process.
source: In summary, analyses revealed mild changes at the most on spine level without clear indication of prevalent alterations related to the culturing process
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the spine morphology data.

claim: Human brain slice cultures may represent a suitable model system to study pathophysiological mechanisms of neurological and neuropsychiatric disease.
source: suggesting that human brain slice cultures may represent a suitable model system to study pathophysiological mechanisms of neurological and neuropsychiatric disease.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the stability data presented.

claim: Whole-cell patch clamp recordings were performed of GFP positive neurons (n=7) and GFP negative neurons (n=13) at matching time points in culture (7-16 DIV).
source: To investigate whether AAV-transduction and GFP expression affected the electrophysiological properties of cortical neurons, we performed whole-cell patch clamp recordings of GFP positive neurons (n = 7) and GFP negative neurons (n = 13) at matching time points in culture (7–16 DIV) and assessed AP half width, resting membrane potential, sag potential and input resistance.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to assess effects of viral transduction.

claim: All recorded neurons displayed normal AP firing upon supra-threshold current injections with either regular spiking patterns (n=7) or fast/adaptive spiking patterns (n=6).
source: All recorded neurons displayed normal AP firing upon supra-threshold current injections with either regular spiking patterns as typical for pyramidal neurons (Figure 8C, n = 7) or fast/adaptive spiking patterns as typical for interneurons (Figure 8E, n = 6) (Ascoli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 8C and 8E and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Most parameters investigated in GFP positive neurons did not differ significantly from values obtained from GFP negative control neurons.
source: Most of the parameters that we investigated in GFP positive neurons did not differ significantly from the values obtained from GFP negative control neurons (Figure 8D and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 8D and F.

claim: In the group of interneurons, a significant reduction of the sag potential at hyperpolarization was found in GFP positive cells compared to GFP negative cells.
source: We found however in the group of interneurons a significant reduction of the sag potential at hyperpolarization compared to GFP negative cells (Figure 8F)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: All other parameters in interneurons were not significantly different between GFP positive and negative cells.
source: while all other parameters were not significantly different
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: There were no significant differences found for any of the parameters in the pyramidal cell group between GFP positive and negative cells.
source: and while there were no significant differences found for any of the parameters in the pyramidal cell group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Virus transduction did not dramatically interfere with neuronal functionality.
source: Taking together these results, virus transduction did not dramatically interfere with neuronal functionality.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the electrophysiological comparison data.

claim: In all examined slices (n=5, 7-15 DIV), pyramidal neurons including dendritic structures and emanating spines could be successfully identified by two-photon microscopy.
source: In all examined slices (n = 5, 7–15 DIV) we could successfully identify pyramidal neurons (Figure 9A displays a representative example) including dendritic structures and emanating spines (Figure 9A1).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 9A and 9A1.

claim: In two experiments (at 7 DIV and 14 DIV), five distinct areas per slice were imaged for 24 hr with image stacks acquired every 30 min.
source: In a second step we asked whether our system would be stable enough to enable time-lapse tracing of dendrites and spines of human pyramidal neurons over a time window of several hours. In two experiments (at 7 DIV and at 14 DIV) we imaged five distinct areas per slice for 24 hr and acquired image stacks every 30 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for time-lapse imaging.

claim: In three areas, a slight shift in the z-axis resulted in an incomplete scan of the neurons and dendrites.
source: While in three areas a slight shift in the z-axis resulted in an incomplete scan of the neurons and dendrites, further technical optimization allowed seven areas to be scanned successfully over the complete time course.
evidence: This describes technical challenges encountered during time-lapse imaging.

claim: Seven areas were scanned successfully over the complete 24-hour time course after technical optimization.
source: further technical optimization allowed seven areas to be scanned successfully over the complete time course.
evidence: This describes the successful outcome after optimization.

claim: Total dendritic length and maximal sholl radius were determined for four neurons at t=0 hours and t=24 hours.
source: To further assess the stability of the system, dendrites of four imaged neurons were manually traced and reconstructed (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A) and total dendritic length and maximal sholl radius were semi-automatically determined for each of the four neurons at t = 0 hours and t = 24 hours.
evidence: This describes the quantitative analysis performed on time-lapse data.

claim: Data revealed reasonably small variability of parameters (mean ± SD: total dendritic length: -3.15 ± 10.87%; maximal sholl radius: 3.12 ± 6.50%).
source: Data revealed reasonably small variability of parameters (mean ± SD: total dendritic length: −3.15 ± 10.87%; maximal sholl radius: 3.12 ± 6.50%)
evidence: This is quantitative data from time-lapse imaging analysis.

claim: The data indicate feasibility of two-photon 24 hr life-cell imaging of human cortical slice cultures.
source: indicating feasibility of two-photon 24 hr life-cell imaging of human cortical slice cultures (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: After further optimization, this approach will enable future studies of spine turnover of individual human neurons within brain slice cultures.
source: After further optimization this approach will enable future studies of spine turnover of individual human neurons within brain slice cultures.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: Questions are raised whether basic anatomic and physiological knowledge as well as disease related pathophysiological data obtained in animal models can be directly translated to the human CNS.
source: The human cerebral cortex is composed of many distinct cell types organized in very specific arrangements according to the highly specialized function of individual cells. Thus, questions are raised whether basic anatomic and physiological knowledge as well as disease related pathophysiological data obtained in animal models can be directly translated to the human CNS.
evidence: This is a statement about the translational gap motivating the study.

claim: The ability to study bona fide human cortical neurons was confined to post mortem studies and acute/fresh post-surgery tissue for a long time.
source: For a long time, the ability to study bona fide human cortical neurons and investigate physiologically and pathologically relevant questions was confined to post mortem studies (Anton-Sanchez et al., 2017; Elston and Fujita, 2014; Huttenlocher et al., 1982) and to acute/fresh post-surgery tissue (Beck et al., 2000; Marcuccilli et al., 2010; Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: With standard procedures, limited viability of resected tissue restricted electrophysiological recordings to a time window of 12-72 hr following surgery.
source: With standard procedures, limited viability of resected tissue restricted electrophysiological recordings to a time window of 12–72 hr following surgery (Wickham et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In recent years, several methods have been incrementally established to keep human CNS tissue functionally intact for extended periods of days to weeks.
source: However, in recent years several methods have been incrementally established by us and other groups to keep human CNS tissue functionally intact for extended periods of days (Ting et al., 2018) to weeks (Eugène et al., 2014; Andersson et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Initial studies based on development of special culturing strategies and complex artificial media revealed feasibility and prompted further investigation.
source: Initial studies based on development of special culturing strategies and complex artificial media revealed feasibility and prompted further investigation and optimization (Eugène et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The authors recently demonstrated that hCSF significantly promotes neuronal viability and long-term survival of human brain slice cultures.
source: We recently demonstrated that hCSF significantly promotes neuronal viability and long-term survival of human brain slice cultures (Schwarz et al., 2017), allowing robust recordings of neuronal network activity for up to 21 DIV.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: The success of the model system critically depends on the maintenance of distinct morphological characteristics of neurons.
source: The success of such a model system would be predicted to not only critically depend on the viability of neurons but also on the maintenance of their distinct morphological characteristics.
evidence: This is a logical inference about requirements for a successful model system.

claim: It remained elusive whether overall neuronal morphology, specifically dendritic complexity, spine distribution and structural features of spines, are preserved throughout the course of culturing.
source: While we had demonstrated general neuronal survival within cultures (Schwarz et al., 2017) it remained elusive whether overall neuronal morphology, specifically dendritic complexity, spine distribution and designated structural features of spines, are preserved throughout the course of culturing.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The present study provides a systematic analysis of pyramidal neurons and interneurons across all cortical layers supporting overall electrophysiological and structural stability throughout the time window up to two weeks in culture.
source: In the present study we now provide a systematic analysis of pyramidal neurons and interneurons across all cortical layers supporting overall electrophysiological and structural stability throughout the time window up to two weeks in culture.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Most parameters quantified in the study did not differ between neurons recorded in acute (0 DIV), early (2-3 DIV) or late stage cultures (7-14 DIV).
source: Specifically, we found that most parameters quantified in this study did not differ between neurons recorded in acute (0 DIV), early (2–3 DIV) or late stage cultures (7-14 DIV).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the electrophysiological and morphological findings.

claim: The resting membrane potential of pyramidal neurons was slightly but significantly lower for neurons recorded in slices at 0 DIV.
source: One exception was the resting membrane potential of pyramidal neurons which was found to be slightly, but significantly lower for pyramidal neurons recorded in slices at 0 DIV.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented earlier.

claim: The change in resting membrane potential might be interpreted as a small initial adaptation of pyramidal neurons to the new conditions in culture.
source: This might be interpreted as a small initial adaptation of pyramidal neurons to the new conditions in culture, particularly since we did not find continued depolarization of resting membrane potential in late stage cultures compared to early stage ones.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed change in resting membrane potential.

claim: Interneurons did not seem to show the effect of changing resting membrane potential observed in pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, interneurons did not seem to show this effect.
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiological data on interneurons.

claim: No major impairment of neuronal function was found in analyzed samples of GFP positive pyramidal neurons (n=7) and interneurons (n=6).
source: Moreover, we measured and compared the properties of GFP positive neurons after viral transduction and found no major impairment of neuronal function in our analyzed samples of pyramidal neurons (n = 7) and interneurons (n = 6), which is in line with a previous study investigating virus transduction in human neurons (Ting et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological comparison data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Subtler alterations from viral transduction cannot be ruled out, particularly given the immense diversity of cortical neurons.
source: Although our data indicate no major interference of viral transduction with neuronal function we cannot rule out subtler alterations, particularly given the immense diversity of cortical neurons, which certainly cannot be represented in its entirety in our samples.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement acknowledging limitations of the study.

claim: This question needs to be further approached in future large-scale studies.
source: This question needs to be further approached in future large-scale studies and respective investigations will benefit from community-based efforts.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Pyramidal neurons of the human temporal cortex show a layer specific dendritic pattern with a gradual increase of total dendritic length of layers 2/3 pyramidal neurons correlating with distance of soma to pia.
source: It has been reported before that pyramidal neurons of the human temporal cortex show a layer specific dendritic pattern with a gradual increase of the total dendritic length (both of the apical and basal compartment) of layers 2/3 pyramidal neurons correlating with the distance of the soma to the pia (Mohan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The study confirmed the layer-specific dendritic pattern in acute/fresh tissue samples.
source: We confirmed this finding in our acute/fresh tissue samples
evidence: This is supported by morphological data from the current study.

claim: The study demonstrates robustness of the layer-specific dendritic pattern throughout the culturing period.
source: and further demonstrate its robustness throughout the culturing period.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data from cultured slices.

claim: The study confirmed a decline in total apical dendritic length at the intersection of layers 3 and 4, corresponding to the presence and survival of spiny stellate neurons.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed a decline in total apical dendritic length in our cultures at the intersection of layers 3 and 4, as demonstrated by Mohan et al. (2015), corresponding to the presence and survival of spiny stellate neurons which are lacking an extended apical dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The gross morphology of apical and basal dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons are considered fairly stable over time in vivo and in vitro in acute slices.
source: While the gross morphology of the apical and basal dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons are considered fairly stable over time in vivo and in vitro in acute slices
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: There is strong evidence that the dendritic fine structure undergoes constant plastic remodeling.
source: there is strong evidence that the dendritic fine structure undergoes a constant plastic remodeling (Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spines have been proven to be plastic and to appear and disappear on time scales of days in the developing and adult brain.
source: Especially the spines have been proven to be plastic and to appear and disappear on time scales of days in the developing (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Lendvai et al., 2000) and adult brain (Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Despite sustained spine turnover, overall spine density has been shown to remain generally stable in adult cortex of mice.
source: On the other hand, despite this sustained turnover overall spine density has been shown to remain generally stable in adult cortex of mice (Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The study detected only small alterations of morphological spine parameters of neurons in cultured slices compared to acute slices along with only a moderate reduction of spine density.
source: We detected only small alterations of the morphological spine parameters of neurons in cultured slices compared to neurons in acute slices along with only a moderate reduction of spine density.
evidence: This is a summary of the spine morphology findings.

claim: The relative stability of spine density is in line with in vivo data showing plastic remodeling with increased spine turnover but overall stability of spine density in response to activity deprivation.
source: Although this is in line with the in vivo data by Trachtenberg et al. (2002), this result may still seem surprising since cultured cortical tissue, disconnected from their surrounding circuitry and thus deprived from outside input, would rather be expected to significantly lose spines. However, these data are in line with Trachtenberg et al. (2002), showing plastic remodeling in mouse pyramidal neurons with an increased spine turnover rate and number of transient spines but overall stability of spine density in response to activity deprivation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spine density findings in comparison to prior literature.

claim: A homeostatic mechanism could explain the relative stability of spine density in adult human brain slice cultures.
source: Such a homeostatic mechanism could explain the relative stability of spine density in adult human brain slice cultures reported here.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed spine density stability.

claim: Future experiments directly determining spine turnover by two-photon live cell imaging will be needed to corroborate the homeostatic mechanism hypothesis.
source: Future experiments directly determining spine turnover by two-photon live cell imaging will be needed to corroborate this hypothesis and to investigate whether alternative or additional mechanisms could have a role in maintenance of spine density in human pyramidal neurons (in slice cultures).
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Such studies of spine turnover are conceivable based on the proof-of-concept data regarding feasibility of live cell imaging for extended time periods.
source: Such studies are indeed conceivable and we provide first proof-of-concept data regarding feasibility of live cell imaging for extended time periods (up to 24 hr) of human brain slice cultures by taking advantage of virally mediated neuronal GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by the two-photon imaging data presented.

claim: Post processing of tissue for GFP signal amplification by immunocytochemistry or tyramide boosting will likely provide structural information surpassing classic biocytin fillings.
source: Post processing of the tissue for GFP signal amplification by standard immunocytochemistry or in combination with tyramide boosting will likely provide structural information even surpassing the one available from classic biocytin fillings.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future improvements.

claim: Depending on promoter specificity, the viral labeling strategy may enable screening for rare human CNS cell types or targeting of certain subpopulations like interneurons.
source: Depending on the degree of cell type specificity of the promoters used to drive the expression of fluorescent proteins this strategy may also enable screening for rare human CNS cell types or targeting of certain subpopulations like interneurons (Dimidschstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications supported by a citation.

claim: It seems intriguing to adopt the same set of tools to study cell autonomous and potentially cell non-autonomous effects of disease related mutated proteins on human CNS cell types.
source: It seems very intriguing to adopt the same set of tools to study cell autonomous and (in light of substantial viral transduction rates) potentially even cell non-autonomous effects of disease related mutated proteins on human CNS cell types of interest.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Adapting state-of-the-art molecular genetic tools for application in human CNS tissue appears increasingly practical and would open new opportunities.
source: Adapting state-of-the-art molecular genetic tools (such as optogenetic and chemogenetic approaches or homologous recombination-driven genetic targeting), currently available in model organisms, for application in human CNS tissue appears increasingly practical and would open completely new opportunities to study both physiological properties of human CNS circuitry and pathological conditions underlying neurological disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications and opportunities.

claim: The study found remarkable stability of morphological and electrophysiological parameters of human pyramidal neurons as cortical network components of slice cultures over 14 DIV.
source: In summary, we found a remarkable stability of morphological and electrophysiological parameters of human pyramidal neurons as cortical network components of slice cultures over a time course of 14 DIV.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's main findings.

claim: The study demonstrates widespread viral transduction of human brain slice cultures, enabling genetic manipulation of adult human neurons under controlled conditions.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate widespread viral transduction of human brain slice cultures, enabling genetic manipulation of adult human neurons under very controlled conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the viral transduction findings.

claim: The model system will be of great value for investigations in viable human neuronal networks such as therapeutic screening, investigation of electrophysiological and structural properties of human CNS circuitry and direct exploration of mechanisms underlying neurological disease.
source: We propose that this model system will be of great value for many investigations in viable human neuronal networks such as therapeutic screening, investigation of electrophysiological and structural properties of human CNS circuitry and direct exploration of mechanisms underlying neurological disease.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the potential applications of the model system.

claim: Human neocortical brain slice cultures were prepared from access tissue obtained from patients undergoing epilepsy surgery.
source: Human neocortical brain slice cultures were prepared from access tissue (cortical tissue outside the epileptic focus, resected in order to gain access to the pathology) obtained from patients undergoing epilepsy surgery.
evidence: This describes the source of tissue used in the study.

claim: Data from 15 patients were collected and included in the study.
source: For this study, we collected and included data of 15 patients (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the patient cohort.

claim: All patients were surgically treated for intractable epilepsy.
source: All patients were surgically treated for intractable epilepsy
evidence: This describes the patient population.

claim: In two patients, histology revealed low-grade tumors (Ganglioglioma WHO Grade I; Oligodendroglioma, WHO Grade II).
source: in two patients the histology revealed low-grade tumors (Ganglioglioma WHO Grade I; Oligodendroglioma, WHO Grade II).
evidence: This describes pathological findings in a subset of patients.

claim: Approval of the ethics committee of the University of Tübingen and written informed consent was obtained from all patients.
source: Approval (# 338/2016A) of the ethics committee of the University of Tübingen as well as written informed consent was obtained from all patients, allowing spare tissue from resective surgery to be included in the study.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Tissue preparation was performed according to published protocols.
source: Tissue preparation was performed according to published protocols (Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the methodology with reference to prior literature.

claim: 250-350 µm thick acute slices were prepared using a Microm HM 650V vibratome.
source: After removal of the pia, tissue chunks were trimmed perpendicular to the cortical surface and 250–350 µm thick acute slices were prepared using a Microm HM 650V vibratome (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the slicing methodology.

claim: Slices were kept in aCSF equilibrated with carbogen for 0.5 hr at room temperature before transfer to patch setups or culture membranes.
source: Afterwards the slices were kept in aCSF equilibrated with carbogen for 0.5 hr at room temperature before they were transferred either to patch setups for acute electrophysiological recordings and biocytin fillings or onto culture membranes for cultivation.
evidence: This describes the tissue handling protocol.

claim: For the first hour following slicing, slices were cultured in NSC media before changing to hCSF.
source: For the first hour following the slicing procedure the slices were cultured in 1.5 ml NSC media (48% DMEM/F-12 (Life Technologies), 48% Neurobasal (Life Technologies), 1x N-2 (Capricorn Scientific), 1x B-27 (Capricorn Scientific), 1x Glutamax (Life Technologies), 1x NEAA (Life Technologies) + 20 mM HEPES before changing to 1.5 ml hCSF per well without any supplements.
evidence: This describes the culture protocol.

claim: No antibiotics or antimycotics were used during cultivation.
source: No antibiotics or antimycotics were used during cultivation.
evidence: This describes the culture conditions.

claim: The plates were stored in an incubator at 37°C, 5% CO2 and 100% humidity.
source: The plates were stored in an incubator (ThermoScientific) at 37°C, 5% CO2 and 100% humidity.
evidence: This describes the culture conditions.

claim: Layer four was clearly visible as a delineated band approximately 1200 µm below the pial surface following DAPI staining.
source: Following DAPI staining of slices (0 DIV - 15 DIV) layer four was clearly visible as delineated band (as has previously been demonstrated by Ting et al., 2018)~1200 µm below the pial surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The distance of the outer margin of layer four from the pia did not differ significantly between tissue slices from three independent surgeries.
source: The distance of the outer margin (edge) of layer four from the pia was assessed for tissue slices prepared from three independent surgeries (P1-3). Mean values were plotted as bar diagrams for comparison (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and did not reveal significant differences.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The distance from pia to layer four did not change significantly over time in culture up to 20 DIV.
source: Furthermore, this distance did not change significantly over time in culture up to the endpoint of analysis at 20 DIV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Human brain slice cultures revealed only a mild decrease of thickness of about 20% over the analyzed three-week period in culture.
source: While mouse organotypic slice cultures are known to flatten out quite extensively throughout the time in culture to the point that they may even become translucent, human brain slice cultures revealed only a mild decrease of thickness of about 20% over the analyzed three-week period in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: hCSF was collected from patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus or idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
source: hCSF was collected from patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) or idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
evidence: This describes the source of hCSF used in cultures.

claim: hCSF of NPH patients exhibits physiological/normal hCSF parameters, undistinguishable from healthy individuals.
source: It is well established and known from daily clinical practice that hCSF of NPH patients exhibits physiological/normal hCSF parameters (lactate, glucose, cell count, protein levels – see Schwarz et al., 2017), undistinguishable from the ones of healthy individuals (Bjorefeldt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: AAV-retro(AAVrg)-hSynapsin-GFP-virus was purchased from Addgene and had a titer of 10^12.
source: AAV-retro(AAVrg)-hSynapsin-GFP-virus was purchased from Addgene (pAAV-hSyn-GFP was a gift from Bryan Roth - Addgene viral prep # 50465-AAVrg) and had a titer of 1012.
evidence: This describes the viral vector used in the study.
